name: Nzadi

catalog_locator: Ch. 3 'Tone': §3.1 Basic Tonal Contrasts p. 37; §3.2 p. 40; end of §3.3 p. 55; §3.4 Intonation p. 56 (pp. 48, 51, 66, 67).
catalog_quote: [p.37] Like most Bantu languages, Nzadi contrasts two tone levels, H(igh) and L(ow). These tones may in turn combine to produce HL (falling), LH (rising) and LHL (rising-falling) contours. In addition, there are contrastive downstepped !H and !HL tones in the language which are mostly derived from contour simplification rules. ... In Nzadi the tone-bearing unit is the syllable. [p.55] What is clear is that tones tend to bunch up on the initial syllable even if the stem is bisyllabic. ... In addition, no matter what tone pattern is assigned to the verb within the paradigm, the second syllable never receives a H (or HL) tone. It is realized L without exception, as if it were not a tone-bearing unit. [p.56] Although Nzadi is a tone language, it is clear that there are phrasal boundary tones and register effects as in yes-no questions. Since intonation has not been studied in great depth, the above few comments will have to suffice.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nzadi is described purely as a two-level (H/L) tone language with syllable as TBU; the grammar makes no claim about word stress or accent. The only prominence-like asymmetry noted is that in bisyllabic (verb) stems tonal contrasts concentrate on the stem-initial syllable and the second syllable is invariably L; 85% of stems are monosyllabic anyway. 'Stress' appears only in reference to donor-language stress being reproduced as final HL on loanwords (p.40).
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords (bulE^ 'blue', sabât 'shoe', kamyç^ 'car', avokâ, kafE^, velô) carry final HL reproducing donor-language stress (p.40). Two bisyllabic verbs o-bán@tsa 'think', o-yún@tsa 'try' are H-L rather than L-L.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone on (mostly monosyllabic) stems with L-toned V-/N- prefixes; phrase level has a H% boundary tone before pause and global pitch raising in yes-no questions (section 3.4). No word-stress domain is defined because no stress is posited.
new_statements.identity_note: Crane, Hyman & Tukumu 2011 is based on a single speaker (Simon Nsielanga Tukumu) from Bundu village, north bank of the Kasai, Bandundu Province; the grammar itself is Glottolog's basis for nzad1234, so identity is exact.

The catalog record for Nzadi (src world-2026-09-17) has an empty rule, which is consistent with a tone language for which no source states a word-stress rule. 40 loanword sentence (the only use of 'stress' in the book) and confirms that Ch. 2 and the index contain nothing on stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nzadi is a two-level (H/L) tone language with HL, LH and LHL contours and contrastive downstep; the tone-bearing unit is the syllable. The grammar makes no statement about word stress or accent: the only occurrence of the word 'stress' in the book (p. 40) says that a final HL on loanwords reproduces the stress of the donor language. The closest thing to a prominence asymmetry is that in bisyllabic stems tones 'bunch up on the initial syllable' and the second syllable of bisyllabic verb stems is always L, 'as if it were not a tone-bearing unit' (p. 55) -- a stem-initial tonal asymmetry the authors do not call stress. Phrase-level prominence is carried by a H% boundary tone and pitch-register raising in yes-no questions (pp. 55-56).
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords (bulɛ̂ 'blue', kɔkɔ̂ 'coconut', pɛpɛ̂ 'papaya', sabât 'shoe', kamyɔ̂ 'car', avokâ 'avocado', kafɛ̂ 'coffee', velô 'bicycle') carry a final HL that 'reproduces the stress of the donor language' (p. 40). In bisyllabic verb stems the second syllable never receives H or HL regardless of paradigm tone pattern (p. 55). Phrase-final H% boundary tone before pause can neutralise L vs LH and HL vs H (p. 55).
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar describes Nzadi [B.865] as spoken by co-author Simon Nsielanga Tukumu, documented in the 2008-2009 Berkeley field methods course; no dialect distinctions bearing on stress or tone are drawn in the sections read. Not opened (not in the works list, paywalled): Hyman 2012, JALL 33:97-117, on Nzadi relative clauses, which would not bear on stress.

sources.note: No word-stress statement. Ch.2 (Sound system, pp.11-36) and Ch.3 (Tone, pp.37-56) describe a two-level H/L tone system with HL/LH/LHL contours and downstep, TBU = syllable; 'Nzadi is a tone language' (p.56). Only mentions of 'stress': p.40, final HL on loanwords 'reproduces the stress of the donor language'. p.55 notes tones 'bunch up on the initial syllable' of bisyllabic stems and the second stem syllable never bears H 'as if it were not a tone-bearing unit' (stem-initial asymmetry, not called stress). p.56: phrasal H% boundary tone and register raising in yes-no questions.

sources.note: In the discussion of whether Proto-Bantu had *H/*L or privative *H/0, cites Nzadi [B865] as a 'most evolved' NW-type language 'which has developed contour tones on its largely monosyllabic stems' (*-bombo > m-bwom LH 'nose', *-lume > o-lum HL 'husband', after Cohen 2011:269). One passage only; no Nzadi inventory or rules. Listed for its tonogenesis-of-contours statement by the grammar's co-author.

Austin, Oliver Bond, Monik Charette, David Nathan & Peter Sells (eds.), Proceedings of Conference on Language Documentation and Linguistic Theory 2, 3-11. London: SOAS. sources.note: Short conference paper (9 pp.) on Nzadi's morphosyntactic reduction; its one tone-relevant passage (section 3, printed p.6 = p.5) states that Nzadi monosyllabic stems derive from longer Proto-Bantu forms by loss of consonants and vowels 'but with preservation of the tones', so that PB trisyllabic *L-H-L surfaces as a monosyllabic LHL contour (examples mwaan 'child', waar 'canoe', lwo 'arm'). No tone inventory, rules or TBU discussion beyond this; the full analysis is ch.3 of Crane, Hyman & Tukumu 2011 (listed here). No stress/accent statement.
sources.venue: Proceedings of Conference on Language Documentation and Linguistic Theory 2
